common_name: Rolly's Favorite Catchfly (Compact Pink-Flowered Campion Hybrid)

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring or early fall in well-drained soil; this naturally occurring Silene hybrid is propagated by division or cuttings rather than seed, since it does not come true.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, since light shade in hot climates keeps the fuzzy basal foliage from scorching. This patented hybrid forms a tidy mounded rosette topped from late spring into summer with clusters of starry, dark pink flowers with white eyes, and shearing spent stems back by half after the first flush encourages reblooming into fall. It is drought-tolerant once established, deer-resistant, and attracts butterflies, making it a reliable edger or rock-garden clump that stays more compact and floriferous than either straight Silene or Lychnis parent.
scientific_name_note: Also sold as Lychnis flos-jovis 'Rolly's Favorite'; believed to be a Silene x Lychnis hybrid of uncertain parentage, patented as PP17,392.

planting.note: Direct sow or start indoors in early spring; established plants can also be divided in spring. This mat-forming rock-garden perennial is valued for flowering later than most alpines.

directions: Grow in moderately fertile, sharply drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun or light shade; heavy or waterlogged soil, especially in winter, quickly rots the crown. This wiry, mat-forming perennial from the Caucasus is prized for its late-season show of magenta-pink, five-petaled flowers held just above narrow semi-evergreen foliage from late summer into fall, when most other rock-garden plants have finished blooming. It works well tumbling over wall tops, edging a border, or filling gaps between paving stones, and has earned the Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit for its reliability. Shear lightly after the first hard frost to tidy the mat for winter.

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in early spring, or in fall in mild-winter climates for earlier bloom; barely cover seed, since light aids germination.

directions: Sow directly in average, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade; nodding catchfly tolerates poor, dry soils and needs no fertilizing. This slender Mediterranean annual produces wiry, often reddish stems of narrow gray-green leaves topped with nodding clusters of small, notched pink or white flowers over a long early-summer season. It is an easy, old-fashioned cottage-garden and edging plant that self-sows readily, and deadheading spent flowers extends bloom while limiting volunteer seedlings the following year.

common_name: Siskiyou Pink Evening Primrose (Siskiyou Mexican Evening Primrose)

planting.note: Set out divisions or container plants in spring in lean, well-drained soil; this selected cultivar spreads by rhizomes and is best propagated vegetatively to preserve its larger flower size and vigor.

directions: Plant in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; overly rich or consistently moist soil encourages rank, floppy growth and faster spread than most gardeners want. 'Siskiyou' is a selected form of pink evening primrose bearing extra-large, two-inch, cup-shaped pink flowers with darker butterfly-wing veining and pale centers that open over a long spring-into-summer season. Like the species it spreads by shallow rhizomes to form a dense groundcover, so give it room in a naturalized bed, dry slope, or container where its vigor can be appreciated rather than fought. It tolerates drought, poor rocky soil, and juglone from black walnut, and draws bees and evening-flying pollinators.
scientific_name_note: Sometimes sold under the synonym Oenothera berlandieri 'Siskiyou'.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light shade; established clumps can also be divided in early spring or fall.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained, rich to moderately fertile soil in full sun to mostly shade. 'Mystica' is a foliage-selected form of native foxglove beardtongue whose leaves emerge green in spring, deepen to glossy burgundy-purple through summer, and finish with a bright red autumn display that persists into early winter. In early summer it sends up sturdy flower spikes of white blooms brushed with purple that draw hummingbirds and bees, held well above the low foliage clump. It is more shade-tolerant than many beardtongues, resists verticillium wilt, and works well as season-long color contrast against silver or chartreuse companions.
